claims.text: Higher baseline DASH score is associated with lower country-level ischemic heart disease mortality during 2010–2021 (MRR 0.914 per 1-SD higher score, 95% CI 0.849–0.983).
Higher baseline AHEI score is associated with lower country-level ischemic heart disease mortality during 2010–2021 (MRR 0.908 per 1-SD higher score, 95% CI 0.838–0.985).
No significant associations with country-level ischemic heart disease mortality are observed for MDS, TJDS, PHDI, or QUANTIDD.
DASH has the highest AIC weight (0.434) among the evaluated dietary scores, followed by AHEI (0.341), with a slightly higher marginal R2 for DASH.
Pairwise comparisons show no statistically significant differences in effect estimates between DASH and AHEI or between either of these scores and the other dietary scores.

evidence.description: MRRs per 1-SD higher score were 0.914 (95% confidence interval, 0.849–0.983) for DASH in multivariable-adjusted linear mixed-effects models across 148 countries.
MRRs per 1-SD higher score were 0.908 (95% confidence interval, 0.838–0.985) for AHEI in multivariable-adjusted linear mixed-effects models across 148 countries.
No significant associations were observed for MDS, TJDS, PHDI, or QUANTIDD in multivariable-adjusted linear mixed-effects models assessing annual IHD mortality.
DASH had the highest AIC weight (0.434), followed by AHEI (0.341), with a slightly higher marginal R2 for DASH.
Pairwise comparisons showed no statistically significant differences in effect estimates between DASH and AHEI or between either of these scores and the other dietary scores.

methodologies.name: Multivariable-adjusted linear mixed-effects modeling of food supply-based dietary scores
methodologies.description: Calculated six dietary scores (DASH, AHEI, MDS, TJDS, PHDI, QUANTIDD) from baseline food balance data and assessed their associations with annual age-standardized IHD mortality over time.
conditions: Outcome evaluated as age-standardized IHD mortality during 2010–2021

limitations.text: Because this was an ecological study, the findings should not be interpreted as individual-level causal effects.
